title: Job 41:9–24
context: The LORD continues speaking. No one dares to rouse Leviathan, so who can stand before its Maker, who owes no one and owns everything under heaven (41:9–11)? The LORD then describes the creature’s strength, armor, fiery breath, and fearless heart (41:12–24). The imagery is poetic and heightened; whatever animal or image lies behind it, the speech presents Leviathan as a creature God made and rules.

verses.text: Behold, the hope of him is in vain. Won’t one be cast down even at the sight of him?
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, the hope of him is in vain.” Arminian readers see the futility of any hope of overcoming Leviathan, which overwhelms even at first sight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see human confidence collapsing before this creature. The verse leads into the central argument of 41:10–11, which turns from the creature to the Creator.

verses.text: None is so fierce that he dare stir him up. Who then is he who can stand before me?
verses.arminianNotes: “None is so fierce that he dare stir him up. Who then is he who can stand before me?” Arminian readers see the argument move from the lesser to the greater: if not Leviathan, then surely not God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the center of the speech. If no one dares rouse a creature, no one can stand before its Maker, and readers in this tradition see here the humbling purpose of the whole poem.

verses.text: Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Everything under the heavens is mine.
verses.arminianNotes: “Who has first given to me, that I should repay him? Everything under the heavens is mine.” Arminian readers see God owing no one anything, while still graciously meeting Job in this speech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear God’s absolute ownership of creation and freedom from obligation. Romans 11:35 is commonly read as echoing this verse, and readers in this tradition stress grace as unearned.

verses.text: “I will not keep silence concerning his limbs, nor his mighty strength, nor his goodly frame.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will not keep silence concerning his limbs, nor his mighty strength, nor his goodly frame.” Arminian readers see the LORD delighting to describe a creature he has made.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God taking pleasure in his works. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD speaks with admiration of what terrifies people, displaying his own wisdom in making it.

verses.text: Who can strip off his outer garment? Who will come within his jaws?
verses.arminianNotes: “Who can strip off his outer garment? Who will come within his jaws?” Arminian readers see more questions stressing that no one can get close enough to harm this creature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the creature’s defenses described as clothing and armor. The rhetorical questions keep returning Job to the limits of human reach.

verses.text: Who can open the doors of his face? Around his teeth is terror.
verses.arminianNotes: “Who can open the doors of his face? Around his teeth is terror.” Arminian readers see poetic language describing the fearsome mouth of Leviathan as gates no one can open.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see vivid imagery of danger. Readers in this tradition take the poetic exaggeration as intended to produce awe, not as a detailed zoological description.

verses.text: Strong scales are his pride, shut up together with a close seal.
verses.arminianNotes: “Strong scales are his pride, shut up together with a close seal.” Arminian readers see the creature’s armor described as tightly sealed, and many readers think of the scales of a crocodile here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of impenetrable armor. A crocodile is one common identification, though readers in this tradition hold any single identification of Leviathan with caution.

verses.text: One is so near to another, that no air can come between them.
verses.arminianNotes: “One is so near to another, that no air can come between them.” Arminian readers see the closeness of the scales emphasizing that no weapon can find an opening.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see detailed admiration of the creature’s design. Readers in this tradition note that the LORD lingers over such detail to display his craftsmanship to Job.

verses.text: They are joined to one another. They stick together, so that they can’t be pulled apart.
verses.arminianNotes: “They are joined to one another. They stick together, so that they can’t be pulled apart.” Arminian readers see the description of unbreakable armor completed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the creature’s defenses as beyond human power to break. The repeated images build a sense of awe that serves the LORD’s purpose of humbling Job.

verses.text: His sneezing flashes out light. His eyes are like the eyelids of the morning.
verses.arminianNotes: “His sneezing flashes out light. His eyes are like the eyelids of the morning.” Arminian readers see poetic hyperbole describing the creature’s spray glinting in the sun and its gleaming eyes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the language as poetic. Some readers see natural description heightened by imagery, while others see the creature drawn with features of ancient sea-monster imagery; the text does not settle it.

verses.text: Out of his mouth go burning torches. Sparks of fire leap out.
verses.arminianNotes: “Out of his mouth go burning torches. Sparks of fire leap out.” Arminian readers see poetic imagery of terror rather than a literal claim that the creature breathes fire.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the language as figurative. Readers in this tradition note that such imagery may draw on pictures of a chaos monster, while the speech insists that this creature is one God made and rules.

verses.text: Out of his nostrils a smoke goes, as of a boiling pot over a fire of reeds.
verses.arminianNotes: “Out of his nostrils a smoke goes, as of a boiling pot over a fire of reeds.” Arminian readers see the image of breath or spray rising like steam, heightened for poetic effect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see vivid comparison drawn from everyday life. Readers in this tradition avoid pressing the image into a literal description, focusing instead on the awe it creates.

verses.text: His breath kindles coals. A flame goes out of his mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: “His breath kindles coals. A flame goes out of his mouth.” Arminian readers see the climax of the fire imagery, which presents Leviathan as terrifying beyond human power to face.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see figurative language intensifying the portrait. Whatever creature or image lies behind it, readers in this tradition stress that the LORD speaks of it as his own creature.

verses.text: There is strength in his neck. Terror dances before him.
verses.arminianNotes: “There is strength in his neck. Terror dances before him.” Arminian readers see strength and dread personified, with terror going ahead of the creature wherever it moves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of overwhelming power. Readers in this tradition note the contrast with Job, whose own terror in his suffering is now set before a far greater power.

verses.text: The flakes of his flesh are joined together. They are firm on him. They can’t be moved.
verses.arminianNotes: “The flakes of his flesh are joined together. They are firm on him. They can’t be moved.” Arminian readers see a description of solid, unyielding strength in the creature’s body.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see firmness emphasized. The repetition of “firm” builds toward the next verse’s image of a heart like stone, underscoring that nothing in Leviathan yields to human force.

verses.text: His heart is as firm as a stone, yes, firm as the lower millstone.
verses.arminianNotes: “His heart is as firm as a stone, yes, firm as the lower millstone.” Arminian readers see fearlessness pictured: the creature has no fear that could be used to master it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of unshakable courage. Readers in this tradition note that the lower millstone was the harder, fixed stone, an image of something that does not move.
